_about: Limits for the sensor quality checks in qc.js. The hard range (fail) and max_step (the biggest believable change between two consecutive readings) are in vocab/variables.json; this file adds the rest. Every number says where it comes from in its basis: 'our estimate' means we chose it from physics and common sense and it is open to change by a teacher, never a measured or published value. Flags never delete or hide a reading and never send an alert.

_sources.ioos_qc: NOAA IOOS QARTOD tests as coded in ioos/ioos_qc (Apache-2.0), commit 524de97: gross range (fail span, suspect span), spike (average of the two neighbours), rate of change, flat line. Its documented example for a slow variable (water level) uses a flat-line suspect time of 10800 s (3 h) and fail time of 21600 s (6 h), and a spike suspect 0.8, fail 3.
_sources.wmo305: WMO-No. 305 (1993), Guide on the Global Data-processing System, chapter 6 (time consistency check), as quoted in the R package dataresqc: the largest change allowed between two observations is, for air temperature, 4 C in 1 h, 7 C in 2 h, 9 C in 3 h; for pressure 3 hPa per hour. Those are hourly values of shaded air, so they only guide our 10-minute limits.

summary.basis: our estimate: only the last 6 hours count, a sensor that has been quiet for 3 hours is the 'sensor quiet' alert's business, and one or two odd points are normal life, so 'check' needs a failed reading, a stuck reading right now, or 3 different suspect readings.

vehicle.basis: our estimate: a sensor on a bus or car sits in sun, in a closed cabin, next to air conditioning and goes through tunnels, so it really does jump (limits x1.5), a parked vehicle may repeat its last reading for longer (flat-line times x2), and a closed car in the Cyprus sun can pass 55 C inside, so for vehicles the temperature fail line is 75 C (the outdoor line of 55 C is in vocab/variables.json) and the suspect line 62 C.

basis.max_step: 8 C between two readings 10 minutes apart is in vocab/variables.json. WMO-No. 305 allows 4 C per hour for shaded air, so this is generous on purpose (sun, doors, air conditioning).
basis.suspect_range: our estimate: outdoor air in Cyprus rarely leaves -5 to 48 C.
basis.spike: our estimate: about 40 % and 75 % of max_step; ioos_qc's own example for a slow variable is suspect 0.8 / fail 3.
basis.flat: our estimate: 0.05 C is one step of a 0.1 C sensor; the 4 h and 8 h are the ioos_qc example times (3 h and 6 h) made a little longer because air-conditioned rooms really do stay steady.

basis.max_step: 25 % between two readings 10 minutes apart is in vocab/variables.json (our estimate, generous: a front or an air conditioner can move it 20 %).
basis.spike: our estimate: about half of max_step for suspect and all of it for fail.
basis.flat: our estimate. At or above 98.5 % the air is saturated (fog, dew) and humidity really does sit there for hours, so that is never called stuck.

basis.max_step: 6 hPa between two readings is in vocab/variables.json. WMO-No. 305 allows 3 hPa per hour; we allow double because a bus can climb a hill (100 m is about 12 hPa). Units: sea-level and low-land sensors only; SenseCAP sends pascals and the server divides by 100.
basis.suspect_range: our estimate: pressure at the schools (near sea level) stays between about 990 and 1030 hPa; 940 to 1050 leaves room for a hill.
basis.spike: our estimate, a third and four fifths of max_step.
basis.flat: our estimate: 0.1 hPa is the size of the noise; a calm high-pressure day can stay within it for a couple of hours but not for 6.

basis.max_step: 1500 ppm between two readings is in vocab/variables.json. Our estimate of a real classroom: 30 children give off roughly 0.4 m3 of CO2 an hour, in a 180 m3 room that is about 500 ppm per 10 minutes with the windows shut, so 1500 leaves a wide margin for a breath held next to the sensor.
basis.suspect_range: our estimate: outdoor air is about 420 ppm, a sensor reading under 350 is off, and 5000 ppm is the usual workplace limit for a whole shift.
basis.spike: our estimate, about a third and four fifths of max_step.
basis.flat: our estimate: a sealed room at night settles near the outdoor level but still wobbles by several ppm, so 'within 1 ppm' for 6 hours is not a real room; the times are long to avoid false alarms.

basis.max_step: 300 ug/m3 is in vocab/variables.json (our estimate; low-cost sensors are indicative only).
basis.suspect_range: our estimate: above 300 ug/m3 for PM2.5 would be a heavy dust storm or a fire next to the sensor, worth a second look.
basis.spike: our estimate; the point must also be at least half as big as the level around it ('rel'), so 80 on top of 400 is not called a spike.
basis.flat: our estimate: a low-cost particle sensor that repeats exactly the same value (a fan that stopped often reads 0 all the time) is stuck; 4 h and 8 h.

basis.suspect_range: our estimate: double the PM2.5 line, because desert dust is mostly coarse.
basis.spike: our estimate, double the PM2.5 limits.

basis.suspect_range: our estimate: the EU information threshold is 180 ug/m3 over an hour, the alert threshold 240.
basis.spike: our estimate, 40 % and 80 % of max_step. No flat-line test: ozone at night can sit near zero for hours.

basis.max_step: 40 dB between two readings is in vocab/variables.json (our estimate: a door slam on a quiet room is about 30 dB).
basis.suspect_range: our estimate: under 25 dB is below what a small microphone can measure, over 110 dB is a siren next to the sensor.
basis.spike: our estimate, a door slam is a normal 30 dB event, so only a bigger one is 'suspect'.
basis.flat: our estimate. At or under 35 dB a small microphone sits at its own floor, an empty quiet room really does read the same for hours, so that is never called stuck; any other exact repeat for 3 h is.

basis.max_step: 100000 lx is in vocab/variables.json: light really can change from full sun to shade in a minute, so the rate-of-change test hardly ever speaks for light, and there is no spike test.
basis.flat: our estimate. Only time while the sun is more than 8 degrees above the horizon (worked out from the date and the time, in Cyprus) counts, so a sensor that reads 0 lx all night, or sits under a steady street lamp, is never flagged; 0 lx or any exact repeat through 3 h of daylight (a covered or stuck sensor) is.

basis.max_step: 15 m/s between two readings is in vocab/variables.json (our estimate).
basis.suspect_range: our estimate: 40 m/s is a hurricane-force gust, far beyond anything for Cyprus.
basis.spike: our estimate: gusts are real, so the limits sit close to max_step (80 % for suspect, 165 % for fail).
basis.flat: our estimate. Calm air (at or under 0.3 m/s) really does give the same reading for hours, so that is never called stuck; any other exact repeat for 6 h is.

not_checked: dust, sea_surface_temperature, wave_height, land_surface_temperature, green_space_share, electricity_renewable_share, dam_fill_level and buses_in_service are model, satellite or statistics values, not readings of one sensor, so they only get the hard range from vocab/variables.json when something asks.
